claims.text: The hierarchical heterostructure is well characterized in alloy produced under standardized conditions.
Grain-boundary characteristics and phase-interface distributions are relevant descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure.
Combining detailed microstructural descriptors with existing mechanical-test data will improve supervised-machine-learning predictions.
The machine-learning algorithm can capture multiscale interactions between microstructural defect distributions and deformation mechanisms.
Learning correlations underlying mechanical response enables rapid prediction of that response.
Including explicit hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors will produce more accurate predictions of Young's modulus in HfNbTiVAl10 than calibrated finite-element simulations.
Including explicit hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors will produce more accurate predictions of yield strength in HfNbTiVAl10 than calibrated finite-element simulations.
Including explicit hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors will produce more accurate predictions of fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 than calibrated finite-element simulations.
The machine-learning method will reduce prediction or simulation time by approximately one order of magnitude relative to established finite-element simulations.
The machine-learning method will predict the mechanical outcomes within approximately 20–30% error margins.
Inaccurate microstructural imaging or descriptor extraction may cause the method to fail.
Extreme anisotropy may cause the method to fail.
Testing far outside the training-data domain may cause the method to fail.
The magnitude of the accuracy and efficiency gains depends on the quality and representativeness of the microstructural and mechanical datasets.
